Every citizen of the Union has the right to move and reside freely within the territory of the Member States, but under the 2004 Citizens' Rights Directive that right is graded according to the length of stay. For up to three months, a citizen needs nothing more than a valid identity card or passport. Beyond three months, the right of residence depends on the person's situation: workers and self-employed people qualify, while students and economically inactive people must have sufficient resources not to become a burden on the host state's social assistance system, as well as comprehensive sickness insurance. Host states may require registration with the authorities after three months.

After five years of continuous legal residence, a citizen acquires the right of permanent residence, which is no longer subject to these conditions. It is lost only through absence from the host state for more than two consecutive years. Family members, including those who are not themselves EU citizens, enjoy rights derived from the citizen's.

Protection against expulsion also increases over time. A host state may restrict free movement on grounds of public policy, public security or public health, but such measures must be proportionate and based exclusively on the personal conduct of the individual concerned. Once a citizen has resided in the host state for the previous ten years, expulsion is possible only on imperative grounds of public security.
statement: Family members who are not EU citizens acquire a right of permanent residence only after ten years.
currentNote: Not supported. The text says family members 'enjoy rights derived from the citizen's' but gives no ten-year rule for them.

passage:
Being an EU citizen brings a practical advantage when travelling outside the Union. If a citizen is in a country where their own Member State has no embassy or consulate able to help, they are entitled to the protection of the diplomatic or consular authorities of any other Member State, on the same conditions as that state's own nationals. The right is set out in the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and repeated in the Charter of Fundamental Rights, and a 2015 directive lays down how it is to be applied.

The assistance covers situations such as arrest or detention, being the victim of a crime, a serious accident or illness, and death, as well as relief and repatriation in an emergency. It can include issuing an emergency travel document to a citizen whose passport has been lost or stolen. The directive also sets out how Member States should cooperate during crises, for example when large numbers of citizens must be evacuated from a conflict zone, with EU Delegations helping to coordinate.

The assisting state may ask the citizen's own Member State to reimburse the costs it incurs, and the citizen can in turn be asked to repay them. The right applies to unrepresented citizens: a traveller whose own country has an embassy able to help must turn to it.
statement: All embassies of the Member States must assist every EU citizen who asks them for help outside the Union.
currentNote: False. The right covers unrepresented citizens only; a traveller whose own country has an embassy able to help 'must turn to it'.

Since 1 January 2021, the EU has had a general regime of conditionality to protect its budget. Under the regulation, the Council can adopt measures such as suspending payments or commitments when breaches of the principles of the rule of law in a Member State affect, or seriously risk affecting, the sound financial management of the EU budget or the protection of the Union's financial interests in a sufficiently direct way. Breaches of the rule of law that have no such link with the budget fall outside its scope; they are dealt with by other instruments.

The procedure is started by the Commission, which must first notify the Member State and give it an opportunity to respond. The Council then decides on a Commission proposal by qualified majority, so no single government can block a decision. Measures must be proportionate, and they can be lifted if the situation is remedied. Importantly, the government concerned remains obliged to make payments to the final recipients and beneficiaries of EU programmes, such as students or farmers, so that they do not bear the consequences.

Hungary and Poland challenged the regulation before the Court of Justice, which dismissed both actions in February 2022. In December 2022, the Council used the mechanism for the first time, suspending about €6.3 billion in commitments under three cohesion programmes for Hungary.
statement: Under the regulation, the Council can suspend all EU funding to any Member State that breaches the rule of law.
currentNote: False. Measures require a 'sufficiently direct' link to the budget and must be 'proportionate'; 'all funding' for any breach goes far beyond this.

EU anti-discrimination law rests largely on two directives adopted in 2000. The Racial Equality Directive prohibits discrimination on grounds of racial or ethnic origin not only in employment but also in social protection, including social security and healthcare, in education, and in access to goods and services available to the public, including housing. The Employment Equality Directive covers discrimination based on religion or belief, disability, age and sexual orientation, but only in employment, occupation and vocational training. Discrimination on grounds of sex is addressed by separate gender equality directives.

The resulting protection is uneven. A person refused a flat because of their ethnic origin can rely on EU law, whereas a person refused the same flat because of their age or sexual orientation cannot, unless national law provides protection, as it does in many Member States. A Commission proposal of 2008 to extend protection beyond employment for these other grounds did not obtain the unanimity required in the Council.

Both directives shift the burden of proof. Once a complainant establishes facts from which it may be presumed that there has been discrimination, it is for the respondent to prove that the principle of equal treatment has not been breached. Both also require Member States to ensure that victims have access to judicial or administrative procedures and that sanctions are effective, proportionate and dissuasive.
statement: EU law protects people against all forms of discrimination when they apply to rent or buy housing.
currentNote: False. Housing is covered for racial or ethnic origin, but the text says age and sexual orientation are not covered in housing by EU law.

In The Logic of Scientific Discovery, first published in German in 1934, Karl Popper proposed a criterion for distinguishing science from non-science. A theory is scientific, he argued, not because it has been confirmed many times but because it is falsifiable: it rules out certain observable outcomes and could therefore be shown to be false. Popper stressed a logical asymmetry. No finite number of observations can prove a universal statement such as 'all swans are white', whereas a single well-established black swan refutes it. Science, on this view, advances through bold conjectures and attempts at refutation rather than by piling up confirmations.

Popper used the criterion to criticise theories that he believed could accommodate any outcome, citing certain versions of psychoanalysis and of Marxist history. A theory that explains everything, he argued, explains nothing.

Critics pointed to complications. Scientists never test a hypothesis in isolation: every prediction also relies on auxiliary assumptions about instruments, initial conditions and background theories. When a prediction fails, it is therefore logically open to blame one of these assumptions rather than the main theory. Historians of science such as Thomas Kuhn added that scientists often keep a successful theory despite anomalies, and that this tenacity has sometimes been productive. Popper accepted that falsification in practice is never conclusive, but he maintained that methodological rules should prevent theories from being rescued by ad hoc adjustments.
statement: Critics showed that testing a scientific theory against observation is logically impossible.
currentNote: Not supported. Critics showed that a failed prediction does not single out the main theory, not that testing is impossible.

Magna Carta was agreed by King John of England at Runnymede in June 1215, under pressure from rebellious barons. It was a practical peace settlement rather than a statement of universal principles: most of its clauses dealt with specific grievances about feudal payments, inheritance, royal forests and the administration of justice. As a peace settlement it failed almost at once. John asked Pope Innocent III to annul it, the Pope declared it null and void in August 1215, and civil war resumed.

The charter nevertheless survived. After John's death in 1216, the regents governing for his young son Henry III reissued it in revised form, and further versions followed in 1217 and 1225. The 1225 version, granted in exchange for a tax, became the definitive text and was confirmed many times by later kings.

Its lasting fame rests on a few clauses, above all the promise that no free man would be imprisoned or deprived of his property except by the lawful judgement of his peers or by the law of the land. In the seventeenth century, opponents of royal power reinterpreted this promise as a guarantee of fundamental liberties, and the charter later influenced constitutional thinking in the American colonies. Today only three of its clauses remain part of the law of England and Wales.
statement: Magna Carta guaranteed fundamental liberties to all inhabitants of England from 1215.
currentNote: False. In 1215 the charter was 'a practical peace settlement rather than a statement of universal principles'; it was reinterpreted as a guarantee of fundamental liberties only 'in the seventeenth century'.

A posted worker is an employee sent by an employer to carry out a service in another Member State on a temporary basis. Posting is distinct from free movement of workers, where a person moves to another country to take up a job there. The Posting of Workers Directive, first adopted in 1996, guarantees posted workers a core set of the host country's terms and conditions, including maximum work periods, minimum paid annual leave and health and safety rules.

A revision that has applied since July 2020 strengthened the principle of equal pay for equal work at the same place. Posted workers are now entitled to the host country's remuneration as set by law or by universally applicable collective agreements, not merely its minimum wage, and reimbursements for travel, board and lodging cannot be counted towards that pay. When a posting lasts more than 12 months, almost all of the host country's labour law applies, with exceptions such as the rules on concluding and terminating contracts and supplementary occupational pension schemes; the period can be extended to 18 months if the employer submits a motivated notification.

Social security follows separate rules. Under the EU coordination regulations, a posted worker generally remains covered by the system of the sending country for up to 24 months, which is shown by a certificate known as the A1 form.
statement: Once a posting passes 12 months, every rule of the host country's labour law applies to the posted worker.
currentNote: False. The limit 'can be extended to 18 months', and even then exceptions remain, such as dismissal rules and supplementary pensions.

In the late 1970s a German retail group wanted to import Cassis de Dijon, a French blackcurrant liqueur, but the German authorities refused because its alcohol content, between 15% and 20%, was below the minimum of 25% that German law required for fruit liqueurs. In 1979 the Court of Justice ruled that the refusal was incompatible with the free movement of goods. A product lawfully produced and marketed in one Member State should in principle be admitted to the markets of the others, even if it does not meet their technical rules exactly.

The Court accepted that national rules may still restrict trade where they are necessary to satisfy 'mandatory requirements', such as the protection of public health, the fairness of commercial transactions or consumer protection. It found, however, that the German rule was not necessary for these purposes: consumers could be informed of the alcohol content by a label, a less restrictive means of reaching the same goal.

The ruling established what became known as the principle of mutual recognition, and it encouraged the Commission to change its approach to harmonisation. Instead of drafting detailed specifications for each product, the EU could concentrate on essential requirements and leave the rest to mutual recognition. A regulation that has applied since 2020 aims to make the principle work better in practice, for example through a voluntary declaration that a product is lawfully marketed in another Member State.
statement: Since 1979, every product sold in one Member State can be sold in all of the others without restriction.
currentNote: False. Products should be admitted 'in principle', and national rules may still restrict trade to satisfy 'mandatory requirements'.

The CE marking appears on many products sold in the European Economic Area, from toys and electrical appliances to machinery and medical devices. By affixing it, the manufacturer declares that the product meets the EU requirements on safety, health and environmental protection that apply to it. The marking is not a sign of quality, nor does it show that a product was made in Europe: goods manufactured in China or the United States must carry it too if they fall within the scope of the relevant legislation.

How conformity is checked depends on the risks involved. For many low-risk products, the manufacturer can carry out the assessment itself, drawing up the technical documentation and signing an EU declaration of conformity. For products such as certain machinery, gas appliances or higher-risk medical devices, an independent 'notified body', designated by a Member State, must be involved. Products that are not covered by any legislation requiring CE marking must not carry it.

Responsibility does not end when the product leaves the factory. National market surveillance authorities check products already on sale and can order them to be withdrawn or recalled. Importers and distributors also have obligations, for example to make sure that the marking and the required documents are present. Online marketplaces have made enforcement harder, because unsafe goods are often shipped directly to consumers from outside the EU.
statement: Most unsafe products found on the EU market were bought by consumers through online marketplaces.
currentNote: Overstated. The text says enforcement is harder because unsafe goods are 'often shipped directly', but gives no share of unsafe products.

The EU defines small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in a Commission recommendation of 2003, and the definition determines eligibility for many EU funding programmes and for lighter treatment under some EU rules. A medium-sized enterprise has fewer than 250 employees and either an annual turnover of no more than €50 million or a balance sheet total of no more than €43 million. A small enterprise has fewer than 50 employees and a turnover or balance sheet total of no more than €10 million, and a microenterprise fewer than 10 employees and no more than €2 million.

The staff ceiling must always be respected, but a firm may choose which of the two financial ceilings to meet. This option exists because companies in trade and distribution typically have high turnover relative to their assets, and a turnover test alone would put them at a disadvantage.

Independence also matters. A company that is part of a larger group cannot simply count its own staff and figures: the data of linked enterprises, and a proportion of those of partner enterprises, are added to its own. Without this rule, a large group could split its activities into many small companies in order to qualify for support intended for genuinely small businesses. SMEs make up around 99% of all businesses in the EU.
statement: A company with fewer than 250 employees always qualifies as an SME under the EU definition, whatever its finances.
currentNote: False. Headcount alone is not enough: a firm must also meet one of 'the two financial ceilings', and the figures of linked and partner enterprises are added to its own.

EU rules on carbon dioxide emissions from new cars and vans do not set a limit for each vehicle. Instead, they set targets for the average emissions of all the new vehicles that a manufacturer registers in the EU in a given year. A manufacturer's individual target depends partly on the average mass of its fleet, so a producer of heavier cars is allowed somewhat higher average emissions than one selling mainly small models. Manufacturers may also form pools and be assessed together, which lets a company with few zero-emission models combine its figures with one that sells many.

A manufacturer whose average exceeds its target pays an excess emissions premium of €95 for each gram per kilometre above the target, multiplied by the number of new vehicles it registered that year. Because the premium applies across the whole fleet, even a small excess can become expensive for a large producer.

The 2023 revision of the rules tightened the targets for 2030 to a 55% cut for cars and a 50% cut for vans, compared with 2021 levels. In 2025, after carmakers warned that they faced heavy penalties, the EU allowed manufacturers to show compliance with their 2025 targets on the basis of their average performance over 2025, 2026 and 2027, rather than for 2025 alone. Critics argued that the change rewarded firms that had been slow to invest.
statement: A manufacturer's emission target is determined solely by the average mass of the new cars and vans that it registers in the EU in a given year.
currentNote: False. The target 'depends partly' on average mass; the text does not make mass the only factor.

Revised EU rules on the rights of rail passengers have applied since June 2023. When a train arrives at the final destination 60 to 119 minutes late, passengers are entitled to compensation of 25% of the ticket price; for a delay of two hours or more, the figure rises to 50%. Railway undertakings may set a minimum threshold, of no more than €4, below which compensation is not paid. Passengers who were already informed of a delay before they bought their ticket have no right to compensation for it.

The revision added a new exception. A carrier no longer owes compensation if the delay is caused by extraordinary circumstances such as extreme weather, a major natural disaster or a major public health crisis, provided that it could not have been avoided. Strikes by the carrier's own staff, however, do not count as extraordinary circumstances. The exception concerns compensation only: it does not remove the carrier's duties to inform and assist passengers and to offer them rerouting.

If the carrier does not communicate rerouting options within 100 minutes of the scheduled departure time, passengers may arrange alternative public transport themselves and claim back the necessary, appropriate and reasonable costs. Member States may exempt urban, suburban and regional services from parts of the regulation.
statement: Member States may exempt any rail service, including long-distance international trains, from the whole of the regulation.
currentNote: False. The text allows exemptions only for 'urban, suburban and regional services' and only 'from parts of the regulation'.

Emissions from road transport, the heating of buildings, agriculture, waste and small industrial installations are not covered by the EU Emissions Trading System for power and heavy industry. They fall instead under the Effort Sharing Regulation, whose sectors together account for around 60% of the EU's domestic greenhouse gas emissions. Since its revision in 2023, the regulation requires these emissions to fall by 40% across the EU by 2030 compared with 2005.

The EU-wide target is divided into binding national targets ranging from a 10% to a 50% reduction. They were set mainly on the basis of gross domestic product per person, so that wealthier Member States carry a larger share of the effort, with some adjustment to reflect where cuts can be made cost-effectively. Each country receives a declining annual emission allocation for every year up to 2030.

Member States have several flexibilities. They can bank surplus allocations for later years, borrow a limited amount from the following year, and buy or sell allocations among themselves. Some may also use a limited quantity of removals from land use and forestry, and a few were allowed to cancel a set number of emissions trading allowances to count towards their targets. Environmental groups have warned that generous use of these options could allow some countries to postpone domestic cuts.
statement: Every Member State must reduce its emissions in the effort-sharing sectors by 40% by 2030 compared with 2005.
currentNote: False. The 40% figure applies 'across the EU'; national targets range 'from a 10% to a 50% reduction'.

The Renewable Energy Directive sets the EU's overall target for the share of energy that comes from renewable sources. Its 2023 revision raised the binding target for 2030 to at least 42.5% of gross final energy consumption, almost double the share recorded in 2020, and added an indicative top-up of 2.5 percentage points that would bring the total to 45%. The target is binding on the EU as a whole rather than on each Member State: countries set out their own contributions in national energy and climate plans, and the Commission can recommend more ambitious efforts if the sum falls short.

Because slow permitting had become a major obstacle, the revision also requires Member States to designate 'renewables acceleration areas' where projects are expected to have limited environmental impact. Inside these areas, the permit procedure for a new installation should in principle not exceed twelve months, against two years outside them, and longer periods apply to offshore projects. Renewable energy plants are also presumed to be in the overriding public interest, which makes it easier for them to benefit from exemptions under certain environmental rules.

Some environmental organisations have welcomed faster permitting but cautioned that acceleration areas must be mapped carefully to avoid harm to sensitive habitats.
statement: Inside renewables acceleration areas, every permit procedure for a new installation is completed within twelve months.
currentNote: False. The procedure 'should in principle not exceed twelve months'; the text does not say every procedure meets this.

The Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, which entered into force in July 2024, extends the EU's ecodesign approach from energy-related products to almost all physical goods placed on the EU market. Food, feed, medicinal products and motor vehicles are among the exclusions. The regulation does not itself set requirements for particular products. Instead, it provides a framework under which the Commission adopts detailed rules, product group by product group, on aspects such as durability, reparability, recycled content and substances that hinder recycling. The first working plan, published in 2025, gave priority to textiles, furniture, mattresses, tyres, iron and steel, and aluminium, among others.

Products covered by such rules will have to carry a digital product passport, giving customers, repairers and authorities access to information about their composition and environmental performance.

The regulation also contains rules that apply without further acts. From July 2026, large companies may no longer destroy unsold clothing, clothing accessories and footwear. Medium-sized companies will be bound from 2030, while micro and small enterprises are exempt. Large companies must also publish each year how many unsold consumer products they discarded and why. Supporters say the ban removes an incentive to overproduce; some retailers argue that donation and resale channels cannot absorb all surplus stock.
statement: Each product sold on the EU market will have to carry a digital product passport under the regulation.
currentNote: False. Only 'products covered by such rules' will need a passport, and some goods are excluded from the regulation altogether.

The EU's revised Ambient Air Quality Directive, which entered into force in December 2024, sets stricter limit values to be met by 2030. The annual limit for fine particulate matter (PM2.5) falls from 25 to 10 micrograms per cubic metre, and that for nitrogen dioxide from 40 to 20. These values move the EU closer to the guidelines published by the World Health Organization in 2021, which are lower still at 5 and 10 micrograms respectively, and the directive provides for regular reviews of whether further alignment is appropriate.

Member States may ask to postpone the 2030 deadline, to 2040 at the latest, if they can show with modelling that the limits cannot be met in time despite appropriate measures, for example because of specific geographic or climatic conditions. Any postponement depends on an air quality roadmap.

The directive also strengthens citizens' rights. People whose health has been damaged by a breach of the rules are entitled to claim compensation, and members of the public must have access to justice to challenge decisions on the directive's implementation. Some industry groups have argued that the new limits will be costly to meet in regions with heavy traffic or industry, while health organisations wanted full alignment with the WHO values from the outset.
statement: Any Member State may decide to delay meeting the new limit values until 2040 if it finds them too costly.
currentNote: False. A postponement requires modelling showing the limits 'cannot be met in time despite appropriate measures' and a roadmap; cost alone is not a ground.

Adopted in 1991, the Nitrates Directive aims to protect waters from pollution caused by nitrates from agricultural sources, mainly fertilisers and livestock manure. Excess nitrogen that is not taken up by crops can leach into groundwater or run off into rivers and coastal waters, where it contributes to eutrophication: the excessive growth of algae, which can deplete oxygen and harm aquatic life.

Member States must identify waters that are, or could become, polluted, using among other criteria a threshold of 50 milligrams of nitrate per litre in groundwater and in surface water used for drinking. The land draining into these waters is designated as nitrate vulnerable zones, although a country may choose instead to apply the measures across its whole territory. In vulnerable zones, farmers must follow action programmes that include periods when spreading fertiliser is prohibited, rules on storing manure and a limit on the quantity of nitrogen from livestock manure that can be applied: 170 kilograms per hectare per year.

The Commission may grant derogations allowing higher amounts in specific conditions, for instance on farms with a long growing season and crops that take up a lot of nitrogen, such as grassland. Member States must report on water quality every four years, and the Commission has repeatedly taken countries to court over insufficient designation or weak action programmes.
statement: Farmers in vulnerable zones can never spread more than 170 kg of manure nitrogen per hectare in a year.
currentNote: False. The text contradicts 'never': the Commission 'may grant derogations allowing higher amounts in specific conditions'.

Before 2022, the EU had no common rules on how full underground gas storage had to be before winter. That changed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, when supply cuts and price spikes exposed the risk of entering the cold months with low stocks. A regulation adopted in June 2022 required Member States with storage facilities to have them filled to at least 80% by 1 November 2022 and to at least 90% by 1 November in later years.

The obligation was adapted to national circumstances. Countries with large storage capacity relative to their consumption did not have to fill beyond a volume equal to 35% of their average annual gas consumption over the previous five years. Member States without storage facilities on their territory had to ensure that the equivalent of 15% of their annual consumption was held in storage in other Member States, or contribute to the effort in another agreed way.

The rules were initially due to expire at the end of 2025. In 2025 they were extended until the end of 2027, but with more flexibility over the timing and level of filling, after traders and some governments complained that a rigid deadline pushed up summer prices by signalling to the market exactly when large volumes had to be bought.
statement: Since 2025, Member States have been free to decide for themselves whether to fill their gas storage facilities.
currentNote: False. The rules were 'extended until the end of 2027'; only the 'timing and level of filling' became more flexible, so the obligation to fill still applies.

The EU Ecolabel, recognisable by its flower logo, was created in 1992. It is voluntary: companies choose whether to apply for it. Criteria are set for product groups such as cleaning products, paints, textiles and tourist accommodation, and they take account of a product's environmental impact throughout its life cycle, from raw materials to disposal. Applications are assessed by competent bodies in each Member State, and compliance is checked by an independent party rather than simply declared by the producer. Food, drink and medicinal products cannot receive the label.

The Ecolabel competes with hundreds of other environmental labels. Studies for the Commission have found that many green claims on the EU market are vague, misleading or unfounded, and that consumers find it hard to tell credible labels from self-declared ones.

A directive adopted in 2024 to empower consumers for the green transition addresses this problem. From 27 September 2026, traders may no longer make generic environmental claims, such as 'eco-friendly', when they cannot demonstrate recognised excellent environmental performance. Nor may they display sustainability labels that are not based on a certification scheme or established by public authorities. Labels such as the EU Ecolabel are therefore unaffected by this ban, while some retailers' own logos may have to be withdrawn or redesigned.
statement: Since late 2026, all environmental claims on products are banned unless they are backed by the EU Ecolabel.
currentNote: False. Only 'generic environmental claims' without 'recognised excellent environmental performance' are banned, and labels based on any certification scheme or set up by public authorities remain allowed.

The EU's Waste Framework Directive ranks ways of dealing with waste in a 'waste hierarchy'. Prevention comes first, followed by preparing for re-use, recycling, other recovery such as energy recovery, and finally disposal, for example in landfill. Member States must apply the hierarchy as a priority order, but they may depart from it for specific waste streams where a life-cycle assessment shows that another option gives a better overall environmental outcome.

The directive and related laws contain binding targets for municipal waste, which covers mainly household waste and similar waste from businesses. At least 55% of municipal waste must be prepared for re-use or recycled by 2025, rising to 60% by 2030 and 65% by 2035. By 2035, no more than 10% may be landfilled. In 2023 the Commission warned several Member States that they risked missing the 2025 recycling target.

Separate collection has been extended over time. Since January 2025, Member States have had to collect textiles separately, and a revision of the directive adopted in 2025 requires them to set up extended producer responsibility schemes, under which producers of clothing and footwear pay for the collection and treatment of the textile waste they generate. The same revision sets targets for reducing food waste by 2030, in processing and manufacturing and in retail, restaurants and households.
statement: Member States must always follow the waste hierarchy, whatever the waste stream or local conditions.
currentNote: False. The text says Member States 'may depart from it for specific waste streams' where a life-cycle assessment shows a better outcome.

The Pay Transparency Directive, adopted in 2023, aims to enforce the principle of equal pay for men and women for equal work or work of equal value. Member States had until June 2026 to bring it into national law. Several of its rights apply to all employers, whatever their size. Job applicants must be told the starting pay, or its range, for the post before the interview, for example in the vacancy notice, and employers may no longer ask candidates how much they earned in previous jobs. Workers may request information on their own pay level and on average pay levels, broken down by sex, for colleagues doing the same work or work of equal value. Contract terms that prevent workers from disclosing their pay in order to enforce equal pay are not allowed.

Reporting duties, by contrast, depend on size. Employers with at least 250 workers must report on their gender pay gap every year, those with 150 to 249 workers every three years, and those with 100 to 149 workers also every three years but only from a later date. Smaller employers have no such duty under the Directive, though Member States may impose one. Where reporting reveals a gap of at least 5% in any category of workers that the employer cannot justify on objective, gender-neutral grounds and does not correct within six months, a joint pay assessment must be carried out with workers' representatives.
statement: Employers with 100 or more workers must report annually on the gender pay gap within their organisation.
currentNote: False. Only employers with 'at least 250 workers' report every year; those with 100 to 249 workers report 'every three years'.

The Platform Work Directive, adopted in 2024, is the first piece of EU law to regulate the use of algorithms in managing people at work. Member States have until December 2026 to transpose it. In 2021 the Commission estimated that more than 28 million people in the EU worked through digital labour platforms, in activities ranging from ride-hailing and food delivery to translation and data entry, and that many of them may have been wrongly classified as self-employed.

To address misclassification, the Directive introduces a legal presumption of employment. Where facts indicating control and direction are found, as determined under national law and collective agreements and taking into account the case law of the Court of Justice, the person is presumed to be in an employment relationship with the platform. The presumption can be rebutted, but it is then for the platform to prove that the relationship is not one of employment. The Directive does not itself list the criteria for triggering the presumption, nor does it automatically reclassify anyone.

On algorithmic management, platforms may not use automated systems to process data on a person's emotional or psychological state or on private conversations. Decisions that significantly affect a person, such as suspending an account, must be taken by a human being. These protections apply to everyone working through a platform, including those who are genuinely self-employed.
statement: From December 2026, everyone who works through a digital labour platform will be treated as an employee.
currentNote: False. The Directive does not 'automatically reclassify anyone'; it creates a rebuttable presumption.

The Youth Guarantee was launched in 2013, when youth unemployment in the EU had risen sharply following the financial and economic crisis. Under it, Member States committed themselves to ensuring that young people receive a good-quality offer of employment, continued education, an apprenticeship or a traineeship within four months of becoming unemployed or leaving formal education. In 2020 the Council adopted a reinforced Youth Guarantee, which widened the target group from people under 25 to people aged 15 to 29. It also placed greater emphasis on reaching young people who are not registered with public employment services, many of whom face multiple disadvantages.

The Youth Guarantee takes the form of a Council recommendation rather than a regulation or a directive, so it is not legally binding. Member States implement it through their own schemes, usually run by public employment services, and the EU supports these efforts with funding, notably through the European Social Fund Plus.

In 2021 the Commission added a related initiative, ALMA, which stands for Aim, Learn, Master, Achieve. The demographic transition model describes how populations change as societies develop. In the first stage, both birth and death rates are high and the population grows slowly, if at all. In the second, death rates fall, thanks mainly to a better food supply, sanitation and medicine, while birth rates remain high, so the population grows rapidly. In the third stage birth rates also decline, as more children survive, education spreads and families choose to have fewer children, and growth slows. In the fourth, both rates are low and the population is roughly stable.

The model was developed from the experience of Western Europe, where the transition took well over a century, and it describes rather than explains: it does not specify why fertility starts to fall when it does, and the timing has varied considerably between countries. Many countries in Asia and Latin America passed through the stages much faster than Europe did.

Some demographers add a fifth stage for countries where fertility has fallen well below the replacement level, which in countries with low mortality is about 2.1 children per woman: the level at which a population replaces itself in the long run without migration. In such countries deaths may eventually exceed births, and the population may decline unless immigration makes up the difference.
statement: Countries where fertility is below 2.1 children per woman always see their population shrink.
currentNote: False. Deaths 'may eventually exceed births', and the population may decline 'unless immigration makes up the difference'.

By the early 1960s three European Communities existed side by side: the European Coal and Steel Community, set up in 1952, and the European Economic Community and Euratom, both operating since 1958. Each Community, however, still had its own executive and its own council of ministers: the coal and steel community was run by a High Authority, while the two newer Communities each had a Commission.

The Treaty on European Union, signed in Maastricht in February 1992, created the European Union and gave it an unusual structure, often described as a temple resting on three pillars. The first pillar consisted of the existing Communities, with the European Economic Community renamed the European Community to reflect its wider scope. Here the established 'Community method' applied: the Commission had the right of initiative, the Council frequently decided by qualified majority, and the Court of Justice could enforce the rules.

The two new pillars worked differently. The second covered a common foreign and security policy, and the third covered cooperation in justice and home affairs, including asylum, immigration, and police and judicial cooperation. In both, decision-making was essentially intergovernmental: the Council generally acted by unanimity, the Commission either shared the right of initiative with Member States or had none, and the Parliament and the Court played only a limited role. Governments wanted to work together in these sensitive areas without handing them over to supranational institutions.

Ratification was not smooth. Danish voters rejected the treaty in June 1992 and approved it in a second referendum in May 1993, after Denmark had obtained several opt-outs, and the treaty entered into force on 1 November 1993. currentNote: False. In some cases the Commission 'shared the right of initiative with Member States', so it was not always excluded.
